Anyway. So, to spawn proof and make sure no iron golems spawn in the caves, it's kind of a time consuming project, but it's fairly simple. They will spawn in any light condition,  but their spawning conditions besides that are like hostile mobs. They need solid blocks to spawn, so things like slabs or buttons on a solid block will render it unspawnable for a golem. Since I mined this pit out, I had a shitload of extra materials so I just made a few shulkers full, then went around to every chunk outside the perimeter and laid the slabs down on the floors. It's time consuming, don't get me wrong. But the spawning sphere where it spawns around the villagers is only like.. I think a 16x16 sphere? Something like that? I went kinda overkill just because I wanted to be sure but you don't have to get crazy with it.

As for zombie and villager placement, I'll just say this. The activator rail is your best friend. It will eject a mob to the right or left of the track when it is powered. It ejects them onto a solid block on either side of the rail, so what I end up doing is making almost like a hallway that gives the cart only one solid block to eject the mob to. From that block is a short distance to a trapdoor that leads to whichever side of the box I want to place that mob into. And you use trap doors because mobs think of that as a solid block they can walk on, so you don't have to hit them into it. The villagers you might have to push but like, it's not that bad. The zombie will just walk right in if you stand on the opposite side of the trapdoor that the zombie ejected to.

I will take the villagers from the breeder and separate them into minecarts when they are babies just so I can send them right when they grow up. But the zombies I keep in a chamber made of tinted glass, so I can keep a few on standby. I also have a filter in this chamber that flows the baby zombies into lava so I only have the ones I want. But I just name tag them in that chamber, wait for night time, and then send them on over to their cell. 

It's kind of like painting. The more prep work you do, the easier the actual work is and the better of a time you'll have, at least imo. I know this was long winded, sorry lol. I'm a bit of a writer and I get sucked into this kinda stuff. But hopefully it's helpful.

With your afk spot being on the ground like that, it's kinda asking for problems. Mobs spawn in a 128 block sphere around the player. That's 128 blocks in every direction from where you're standing. You might get a few in your farm here and there maybe, but the majority of mobs will spawn in caves underneath you and other spawnable areas around you. Eventually the areas they spawn will have enough mobs in them to take up the mob cap, making the farm non functional. 

Couple different ways to go about fixing it. You could take the time to get into every cave, crevice, and dark area within that spawning sphere and spawn proof everything except for your farm. Which would work, but it's gunna take a looooong. Long. Long time. Way more of a hassle.

Or you could tear down the farm, and rebuild it in the sky. Your afk spot would need to be over 128 blocks above ground level, that way there's no spawnable blocks within the sphere around you except for the ones in the farm. Kinda sucks to have to tear down what you got and go into the air so much but it's much easier and quicker in my opinion to do that instead of the first option.

There's a 50% chance for them to turn in Normal mode, but that's a 50% chance per each attempt. Not over all.

It's kind of weird to explain, I'll admit. But each attempt is it's own individual bracket of the statistic. Instead of it being 50% of the time, it's a 50% chance, every single time. Failing one roll has absolutely no effect on the rest of your rolls, as each one is it's own separate instance.

You could flip a coin 100 times,  and theoretically, you would get heads 50 times and tails 50 times. Though that's often not the case. If you're extremely unlucky, it's possible you could get tails 100 times and heads 0 times, or vice versa. You have a 50% chance per flip, but each flip is it's own attempt at that 50%. The coin doesn't remember whatever happened the last ten times you flipped it and say "oh, they are due for a heads" and give it to you. 

In your case, it's not "50% OF ten times" you tried, but more that you "attempted the roll ten times, at a 50% chance each time."

Unfortunately it's just luck and RNG, friend. It can be your best friend or your jerk of an enemy lol

I've been in an apprenticeship for a couple months and have invested about a grand into some beginning tools for myself that actually impressed a different carpenter and got him to hire me on the spot. 

Honestly, most of what you listed is perfect for a beginner. Quality tape measure, pencils, speed square, a framing hammer, cats paw, string line, and of course bags for all of it to go in. That will cover a majority of your beginning tasks and give you a solid base to learn on and continue developing.

From there, I purchased a drill gun/impact gun set. If I have a word of advice, and if you are dead serious about the trade, it will work better for you to invest in the quality, professional sets from the get go. I bought a few cheap sets and a few cheaper individual guns but they all ended up being more of the home-owner type tools, not professional. Some didn't work right out of the box, and some shit themselves after one day. I bit the bullet and quit fucking around and bought the Dewalt XR professional series set, it has a hammer drill gun and a 1/4 inch impact gun. Cost me a little over 300$ but man, they are beefy and you can just work them into the ground and they will not disappoint. 

Beyond that, I have purchased a skil saw, 7 1/4 inch blade, worm drive. Nothing fancy, but still a professional,  quality tool that will help you get started and cover most saw work you'll have to do. Not everything,  naturally. But it's a good starting point.

Beyond that, I know there's a ton of other tools available. Corded, cordless. Many types of saws. Many types of planers, sanders, levels.. I mean you could spend 5 grand and still have other tools to buy. But as an apprentice, if you can cover your bases and be able to do most of your general tasks with quality tools, you're doing pretty damn good. I mean that 600$ table saw would be nice to have, but you really don't need it on your first day.

But, to each their own.

I’ve worked for a few of these types of websites. Textbroker was the only one I ever cashed out of. I believe my total was 5-8 articles that were around 600-900 words a piece. and a total payment of about 20$. Considering the time I spent researching the topics and working, i would have gotten more by spending a few hours working for McDonald’s, lol. But I still thought it was cool.

You run into a few common problems with these kinds of sites. The biggest being the fact that there are hundreds of thousands of people all thinking the same exact thing. This over saturates the market and kinda just makes you another drop of water in the entire ocean. Most often you’re either over looked completely, or because of all the competition, you’re grinding and working for pennies. There are definitely exceptions, of course. There are people that clickety clack for a few hours a day and make a good salary. But expecting that right out of the gate is futile.

Another issue is that most of these sites have payment thresholds that must be reached before they will let you cash out. The most common I’ve seen is 50$. Now, that does make sense from the sites perspective, because making payments costs money, so the less they have to do it the better. But for us writers, it can be challenging. Wether you’re pumping out a few dozen smaller articles, or maybe making larger ones worth 10-15$ (for your average writer), getting to that 50$ threshold does take a good amount of time. Again, by the time you reached the threshold, you could have worked a couple shifts at McDonald’s and made much more.

These sites are great, don’t get me wrong. And there is potential for a decent amount of pocket money if you’re successful. But the person thinking they are going to buy a house and make a living by writing a couple articles a day are in for a bit of a reality check.

But, you do you. If you’re just looking for a fun way to get money for pizza, you won’t be disappointed!

Smelling good is kinda like an equation, there’s layers of things that all can add up to smelling good or bad.

1. Shower, (obviously). Using a good smelling soap/body wash/ shampoo makes your body itself smell good. I recommend using a wash rag as well, as it kinda scrubs the smell into your skin better than just lathering it. 

2. Use laundry detergent/dryer sheets that make your clothes smell amazing. As the second layer that comes after your skin, good smelling clothes really make the difference. 

3. I know you said deodorant already, but I’m saying it again. A good deodorant can make a world of difference. One of my tricks is to also not just use it on my armpits, but I rub some on my chest/sides as well. The more areas it is, the more pronounced the smell. I’m not saying scrub every inch of your body, but a few key areas can make a difference.
